extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; educated early-18th-century literate public interested in literature, morals, and manners
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of short moral and literary essays (The Spectator) discussing what constitutes 'great genius', the social value of country wakes and bodily exercises, the vice of inconstancy, and methods of consolation under affliction. The page offers prescriptive judgements about character, taste, and conduct rather than formal technical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great natural genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Those few who, 'by the meer Strength of natural Parts, and without any Assistance of Arts or Learning, have produced Works that were the Delight of their own Times, and the Wonder of Posterity.' They appear 'nobly wild and extravagant' and are 'infinitely more beautiful than all the Turn and Polishing of what the French call a Bel Esprit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Homer, some Eastern writers, certain Ancients and Pindar. Expect failures in nicety and correctness (indecent or rough similitudes), but value the sublime impulse. Anti-pattern: deriding ancient irregularities while failing to relish their sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refined genius formed by art
rubrics_metrics.description: A second class of great geniuses are 'those that have formed themselves by Rules, and submitted the Greatness of their natural Talents to the Corrections and Restraints of Art' (examples: Plato, Aristotle, Virgil, Tully, Milton, Bacon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their greatness shows 'after a different Manner' — like rich soil 'laid out in Walks and Parterres' by a gardener. Danger: they may 'cramp their own Abilities too much by Imitation' and lose originality. Advice: imitation of the best authors cannot equal a good original; keep something peculiar and entirely your own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of genius and risk of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest genius 'runs through the Arts and Sciences, takes a kind of Tincture from them, and falls unavoidably into Imitation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While cross-disciplinary reach is a mark of greatness, it tends to induce imitation of varied models; authors should beware forming themselves wholly upon models and thereby losing original voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern — artificial Pindaricks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is ridiculous when 'Men of a sober and moderate Fancy' imitate Pindar by copying 'Irregularities by Rule' and 'by the little Tricks of Art straining after the most unbounded Flights of Nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to manufacture the wild inspiration of Pindar through formulas or mannerisms. Imitation of monstrous or singular works 'by Rule' yields mere distortion and grimace, not the divine impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misapplied perseverance/wasted talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Great application and perseverance may be 'thrown away upon Trifles' (example: a shepherd perfect at tossing eggs who, by right application, 'might have made him a greater Mathematician than Archimedes').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a person's genius also by the worthiness of its application; encourage directing assiduity toward significant pursuits rather than trivial accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of country wakes and bodily exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Country wakes (holiday assemblies) bring 'a promiscuous Multitude' together where people show themselves in exercises (running, wrestling, cudgel-playing, football) to 'gain the Approbation of the Lookers on' and demonstrate health and fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive effects: promote bodily strength, emulation, courtship/marriage (winners gain favor), community cohesion, and (historically) military readiness (longbow practice). Suggested improvement: channel emulation into handicraft/trade prizes. Anti-patterns: suppressing such customs (Puritan/assize suppression) removes social benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and civic utility of public contests
rubrics_metrics.description: The spirit of emulation in wakes could be directed for public good — e.g., annual prizes for excellence in handicraft trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use customary competitions and prizes to encourage skills useful to the commonwealth rather than merely for pastime; view prizes (like the beaver-hat) as honorable community tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy as a moral requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconstancy (especially regarding religion or party) 'makes a Man appear so contemptible and little in the Eyes of the World.' A man's conviction in great articles of life 'ought to be very strong' and must seem free of worldly advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid being 'hated by those he left' and 'not heartily esteemed by those he comes over to,' ensure changes of side appear motivated by principle and honour. Maintain steadfast adherence to one great end as the chief aim of pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid irresolution — settle on an ultimate aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Irresolution among competing motives (ambition, interest, inclination, reason) causes 'the greatest and most universal Causes of all our Disquiet and Unhappiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better to choose and adhere to a mode of life that is not perfect than to grow old without a settled choice. Be guided by reason; if one adheres to a principal design (e.g., virtue) other goods (wealth, reputation) should be subordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts of consolation over rules for happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Enquiries after happiness are less useful than 'the Arts of Consolation, and supporting one's self under Affliction.' Aim for contentment rather than the pursuit of excessive happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To support oneself under affliction: read moral authors who give instances of calamity (to fortify), consider society of sufferers, compare one's distress with greater calamities to gain perspective, and turn to devotion if inclined. Monsieur St. Evremont's opposing view (seek diverting authors like Don Quixote) is noted but the author prefers authors who show human distresses (Plutarch, Seneca).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for consoling a broken heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific consolations for a disappointed lover: recourse to devotions, reading good books, comparing one's misfortune with greater calamities elsewhere, and reflecting that present misfortunes may prove blessings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use religious and moral reflection; seek the company of virtuous sufferers for sympathy; prefer consolations founded 'upon Reason, and established in good Sense' though consolations from other religions may still have effect.
